articles.title: Counterfeit Spirits in Vietnam: How to Drink Safely
articles.excerpt: Methanol in fake spirits has killed travellers in Vietnam, and the bottles have come from ordinary bars and shops. The rules for avoiding it are simple and they are not the ones you have heard.
articles.content:
Vietnam is a cheap and sociable place to drink, and most of the drinking in it is beer. The risk is in spirits. Counterfeit or home-distilled liquor containing methanol circulates in Vietnam, as it does elsewhere in Southeast Asia, and it has caused deaths among tourists. This is not a reason to stop drinking. It is a reason to understand where the risk lives, because it is narrower than the headlines and wider than the common advice.

What the risk actually is

Methanol poisoning from alcoholic drinks is a documented hazard in Vietnam. The UK government's travel advice states that there have been deaths and serious illness from drinks containing methanol, bought in licensed bars, shops and hotels in tourist areas, that even a small amount can kill, and that methanol cannot be detected by taste or smell. The State Department's Vietnam page does not address it; the British page is the official source that does.

The mechanism is ordinary fraud. A bottle with a known label is refilled with cheap distilled alcohol, or a bar buys spirits from a supplier whose stock was never genuine, or a batch of local rice liquor is distilled badly. Methanol is a by-product of bad distillation and an adulterant in cheap fakes, and it is poisonous in quantities that ethanol is not.

The part most advice gets wrong

You will read that a drink which tastes harsh or sweet is suspect. The government advice is explicit that taste and smell do not reveal methanol, so a drink that tastes fine is no reassurance and a drink that tastes rough is not evidence. The protection is in where the bottle came from, not in the glass.

Where the risk is low

Beer is the low-risk drink in Vietnam. A canned or bottled beer opened in front of you, from any of the national brands, carries essentially no methanol risk, and the same is true of the fresh draught beer poured from kegs on street corners in Hanoi, which is brewed, not distilled. Wine from a sealed bottle with an intact seal is in the same category. If you drink only those, this article is background.

Why beer is different

Methanol comes from distillation or adulteration. Beer is not distilled and is not worth faking at its price. Spirits are both.

Where the risk is higher

Spirits poured from an open bottle are the exposure: cocktails, mixed drinks, shots and free-pour measures in places where the bottle's history is unknown. The cases that reach the news cluster in backpacker nightlife areas and beach resorts, where cheap cocktail deals, drinks in buckets and all-you-can-drink promotions are sold at prices that do not cover genuine spirits. A cocktail that costs less than the beer next to it is being made from something.

Home-distilled rice liquor is the other source. It is offered with real hospitality in the countryside and at Tet, it is usually fine, and it is unregulated. A glass with a family is a judgement call most travellers make in favour of the family. A night on it in a bar is not.

The branded bottle is not proof

The whole point of the fraud is the label. A famous name on a bottle behind a bar tells you what the bar paid for the label, not what is in it.

Rules that work

Drinking safely in Vietnam comes down to four habits. Drink beer or sealed wine by default. Drink spirits in established hotel bars and restaurants whose supply chain is their reputation, not in promotion bars. Buy any bottle you take home or to a party from a supermarket or a chain store, not a corner shop or a street seller. Decline anything free-pour, bucket-sized or implausibly cheap, however good the night is going.

None of those is a hardship. Together they remove nearly all of the exposure, and they leave the drinking culture intact, because the drinking culture is beer on a plastic stool.

Spiked drinks are a separate problem

The same official advice tells you to buy your own drinks, keep them in sight and be wary of drinks or snacks from new acquaintances. That is about drugging, not methanol, and the precaution is the same one you would take in any nightlife district at home.

If someone is ill

Methanol poisoning does not look like methanol poisoning at first. Symptoms can be delayed for many hours after drinking and start as a hangover: headache, nausea, confusion, dizziness. The distinguishing sign is the eyes: blurred or snowy vision, sensitivity to light, or loss of sight. Breathing difficulty follows. Anyone who drank spirits the night before and has visual symptoms needs a hospital immediately, not sleep and water.

Call 113 for traffic police, 115 for an ambulance, or go directly to an international clinic. Treatment exists and works when it is early, and it is a hospital treatment; there is no home remedy. In Hanoi, a government-published list names Family Medical Practice, International SOS and Raffles Medical as English-speaking clinics with emergency medicine, and the same groups have clinics in Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang. Tell the clinic what was drunk and where; it matters to the treatment and it may save the next person.

Insurance

Poisoning from a drink is an illness, not an accident, and it is covered by ordinary travel medical insurance; the policy exclusions to read are the ones about intoxication, which vary. Carry the insurer's emergency number with the local ones.

articles.title: Dog, Balut and Field Rat: The Menu Words to Know Before You Order
articles.excerpt: Nobody is going to serve you dog meat by accident. A handful of dishes do surprise visitors, and knowing their names in Vietnamese is the whole of the precaution.
articles.content:
Vietnam has a short list of dishes that American visitors are nervous about, and a long list of articles that treat them as a dare. The useful version is simpler. These dishes are real, they are mostly a specialist taste rather than everyday food, and they are not hidden in the things you will actually order. The precaution is to recognise a few words on a sign or a menu, and to know which of them are a matter of squeamishness and which are a matter of health.

The words, in one place

The Vietnamese menu words that most often surprise visitors are: thịt chó (dog meat), thịt mèo (cat meat), hột vịt lộn or trứng vịt lộn (balut, a fertilised duck egg), chuột đồng (field rat), rắn (snake), tiết canh (raw blood pudding), and the group of insect and larva dishes such as dế (crickets), nhộng (silkworm pupae) and đuông dừa (coconut worms).

Add thịt dê (goat), ếch (frog) and ốc (snails), which surprise some people and are ordinary food here, and you have the whole vocabulary.

Signs are the main place you will meet these words, because the specialist restaurants advertise their speciality in large letters. A menu in a mixed restaurant lists the ordinary dishes first and the specialities, if any, at the end.

The euphemism to know

Dog restaurants often do not write thịt chó on the sign. The common euphemism is cầy tơ, and a sign reading that is a dog-meat restaurant. If you see it, you know what the place is; if you do not, nothing on an ordinary menu is dog.

Dog and cat

Dog meat is eaten in Vietnam, mostly in the north and traditionally at the end of the lunar month, in specialist restaurants with their own clientele, and it has been in decline for years under pressure from animal-welfare campaigns, younger Vietnamese attitudes and public-health concern about rabies and stolen pets. A tourist eats it only by walking into a restaurant that sells it and ordering it.

It does not appear in pho, in a rice plate or in a banh mi.

Cat is rarer still and the same logic applies. The reason to know the words is not to avoid being tricked, which does not happen, but to understand what the restaurant with the big sign and the cages outside is, so that you can walk on without a scene.

Your feelings about it

Many Vietnamese share them. It is a divided question inside the country, not a national custom you are being asked to respect, and declining it needs no explanation.

Balut

Hột vịt lộn is a duck egg incubated for two to three weeks and then boiled, eaten from the shell with salt, lime, chilli and a sharp herb, usually in the evening with beer. It is a street snack across Southeast Asia, famous in the Philippines, and in Vietnam it is sold from stalls that offer nothing else, often lit by a single bulb with a tray of eggs and a pile of herbs.

It tastes like a rich egg with a texture most Westerners find difficult because of what they can see.

It is a health non-issue when freshly boiled, and it is a matter of nerve rather than risk. The word on the sign is the whole warning: an egg stall selling vịt lộn is selling this and not a hard-boiled egg.

Field rat and snake

Chuột đồng is the rice-field rat of the Mekong Delta, trapped in the paddies after the harvest, grilled or roasted, and regarded locally as clean country food quite distinct from the urban animal. It appears on menus in the delta and in southern specialist restaurants, labelled plainly, and nowhere else.

Rắn is snake, served in the north and around Hanoi in restaurants that make a ritual of it: the snake is killed at the table, the blood and bile are mixed into rice liquor for the guests, and the meat is cooked in several dishes.

Neither reaches an ordinary table. The snake restaurants in particular are sold to visitors as an experience, and the thing to know before you accept an invitation is what the ritual involves and that the snakes used are, in many cases, protected species.

Snake wine

Rượu rắn is rice liquor with a snake, a scorpion or both steeped in the bottle, sold as a tonic and as a souvenir. It is a souvenir that US customs is likely to seize, because the animals in it are often protected species, and it is also an unregulated spirit, with the methanol risk that attaches to any home-distilled liquor.

The one that is a health question

Tiết canh is the dish on this list to decline on medical grounds rather than taste. It is fresh animal blood, usually pig or duck, set into a pudding with herbs and peanuts and eaten raw. Raw blood carries whatever the animal carried, and the dish has been linked in Vietnam to serious bacterial infections and to bird flu in the years when it circulated. Vietnamese health advice discourages it for Vietnamese people.

Visitors have no reason at all to eat it.

Offal and the ordinary

Lòng is offal, and a bowl of pho or a rice-noodle soup may offer it as an option, cooked. Óc is brain. Both are ordinary cooked food. Being squeamish about them is a preference, and declining them is as simple as pointing at the plain beef instead.

How to order without worry

Ordinary Vietnamese restaurants and street stalls sell pork, chicken, beef, fish and vegetables, and they say so. If you can recognise gà (chicken), bò (beef), heo or lợn (pork), cá (fish) and rau (vegetables), you can order anywhere, and the specialist words above will never appear in front of you unless you walk into the specialist's door. The fear of being served something unknowable is the one thing on this list that has no basis.

The food is labelled, the sellers are proud of it, and the only way to eat dog in Vietnam is on purpose.

articles.title: The Mekong Delta Beyond Can Tho: Vinh Long, Sa Dec, Tram Chim and Chau Doc
articles.excerpt: The standard delta trip stops at the floating market. A second line of towns runs west to the Cambodian border with homestays, birds, Khmer pagodas and a river crossing, and it is where the delta gets good.
articles.content:
Almost every Mekong Delta trip sold from Ho Chi Minh City follows one line: My Tho or Ben Tre for a day, Can Tho and the Cai Rang floating market for a night. That line is the delta's front porch. West and south of it there is a second line of towns, each with one thing worth a day, that ends at the Cambodian border. This is the delta that people who liked the first trip go back for, and it can be done the first time if you give it the days.

The second line, in order

The towns beyond the standard circuit run roughly west from Vinh Long: Vinh Long itself and its river islands for a homestay, Sa Dec for a colonial house and flower gardens, Cao Lanh and the Tram Chim wetland for birds, and Chau Doc on the border for a hill temple, floating fish farms, a Cham village and the boat to Cambodia. Tra Vinh, south of Vinh Long, adds the Khmer pagodas.

End to end it is five or six days; any one piece is a day.

The road network reaches all of them and the buses run, but English thins quickly west of Can Tho and the buses are slower and rougher than the coach to Can Tho. A car with a driver for the stretch, or a small-group tour that runs this route, turns a patient trip into a comfortable one.

How it connects to the standard trip

Vinh Long is on the way to Can Tho, so the second line starts before the first one ends. A common shape is a night on an island near Vinh Long, then Can Tho for the market, then the road west to Chau Doc. The Can Tho night stays; the second line wraps around it.

Vinh Long: the homestay night

Vinh Long is the delta's homestay town, where the river islands opposite the city have family-run houses in orchards that take guests for the night. You cross by ferry, cycle the lanes between fruit trees and canals, eat with the household, and in the morning a boat takes you to the Cai Be floating market before the activity thins.

It is quieter and more domestic than Can Tho, and for most visitors it is the single best night in the delta.

The homestays range from a mattress in the family room to private bungalows with bathrooms. Ask what you are booking. The orchards are at their best in the fruit months of early summer.

Sa Dec

Sa Dec, a short drive on, is a river town with a nursery-garden district that supplies flowers to the whole south and a Chinese merchant's house that readers of Marguerite Duras will recognise as the setting of her Mekong love story. It is a half day on the way to Cao Lanh, not a destination in itself, and it is at its best in the weeks before Tet when the gardens are in full production.

Tram Chim: the birds

Tram Chim national park, north of Cao Lanh, is a wetland of flooded grassland and cajuput forest that holds some of the delta's last large bird populations, including, in season, the sarus crane. You see it from a boat along the dykes and from a watchtower, and the birds are active early; by late morning the heat has flattened the day. It needs a dawn start from Cao Lanh or Sa Dec and a guide who knows the water levels.

Tram Chim is the piece most worth skipping if birds mean nothing to you and the piece most worth the detour if they do. The cranes are seasonal and not guaranteed. The egrets, storks and the landscape are there all year.

Health note for the wetlands

The CDC describes malaria in the Mekong delta as rare and rural, with no transmission in the cities, which is why standard delta trips do not involve tablets; a dawn in a wetland is still a dawn among mosquitoes, so repellent and sleeves are the sensible precaution. Dengue is the mosquito illness that actually circulates in the south, and the same precaution covers it.

Chau Doc: the border town

Chau Doc sits on the Bassac river at the Cambodian border and is the most interesting town on the line. Sam Mountain rises behind it with a cluster of temples and a view across the flat border country into Cambodia. On the water there are floating houses with fish farms beneath them, and across the river a Cham Muslim village with a mosque, a reminder that the delta is not only Vietnamese.

The Tra Su cajuput forest, a short drive out, is a flooded forest seen by rowboat from under the trees.

Chau Doc is also where the second line can leave Vietnam, by fast boat up the river to Phnom Penh, which turns a transfer into a day of the trip.

The crossing has a visa catch

The river crossing does not accept a Cambodian e-visa. Crossing into Cambodia on a Cambodian e-visa works only at Bavet, the road crossing on the Ho Chi Minh City to Phnom Penh bus route; at the river post you need a Cambodian visa obtained by another route, and your Vietnamese e-visa must name the river crossing as its exit. Check both before you book the boat, because neither can be fixed at the post.

Tra Vinh: the Khmer delta

Tra Vinh, south of Vinh Long, is the town for the delta's Khmer population, with dozens of Theravada pagodas in the Cambodian style set among tall trees, a Khmer cultural museum and a pond that is a local pilgrimage site. It is flat and quiet and best done by bicycle in a day, and it is almost never on a tour. It fits as a day out of Can Tho or as a stop between Vinh Long and the coast.

Putting the days together

Three days: Vinh Long homestay, Can Tho market, Chau Doc. Four: add Tram Chim between Can Tho and Chau Doc with a Sa Dec stop. Five or six: add Tra Vinh and leave Vietnam by river. Any version is a different trip from the coach day out of the city, and whether that longer version is worth its days against the rest of your route is one of the trade-offs the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.

Book a multi-day Mekong Delta tour that names these towns, or arrange a driver from Can Tho and build it yourself.

articles.title: Eating in Vietnam with a Peanut or Shellfish Allergy
articles.excerpt: Peanuts and shrimp are everywhere in Vietnamese cooking and often invisible. A serious allergy does not rule out the trip, but it changes how you order, where you eat and what you carry.
articles.content:
Vietnamese food is built on two things that cause the most serious food allergies: peanuts, scattered over salads, noodle bowls and dipping sauces, and shellfish, in the form of shrimp and the fermented shrimp paste that flavours dishes you would never guess. A peanut or shellfish allergy does not make Vietnam impossible. It makes it a country where you need to know the words, the hiding places and the eating strategy, and where the cart is a different proposition from the restaurant.

The words you need

The sentence that matters is "tôi bị dị ứng", which means "I am allergic", followed by the thing: "đậu phộng" is peanut in the south and "lạc" in the north; "tôm" is shrimp, "cua" is crab, "hải sản" is seafood in general, and "mắm tôm" and "mắm ruốc" are the fermented shrimp pastes. "Không" means "no" or "without", so "không đậu phộng" asks for no peanuts.

Say it, show it written, and watch the face: understanding is not the same as the kitchen hearing it.

Carry a printed card in Vietnamese that states the allergy, that it is serious, and that the dish must contain none of the ingredient and must not be cooked in oil or a pan used for it. Allergy-card services sell these; a Vietnamese-speaking friend can write a better one. Hand it over before ordering, not after.

Tones and the word for "no"

Vietnamese is tonal, and a mispronounced word is a different word. The card exists because your pronunciation will fail at the moment it matters most. Point at it.

Where peanuts hide

Crushed roasted peanuts are a finishing garnish across Vietnamese cooking, and they are added at the last moment by hand, which means the dish arrives with them unless the kitchen was told. The common places are the dipping sauce for fresh spring rolls, which is often hoisin thickened with ground peanuts; grilled-pork noodle bowls; green papaya and other salads; sticky rice sold for breakfast with a peanut-sesame sprinkle; and the sweet dessert soups.

Peanut oil is not the standard cooking oil, but the garnish is standard.

Peanuts are usually visible, which is the mercy. A bowl can be inspected and a garnish declined. The sauce is the trap, because the peanut is ground into it.

Dishes that are usually safe from peanuts

Pho and most clear noodle soups, grilled meats and fish without the sauce, steamed rice dishes, and the baguette sandwiches, which carry pâté and pickles but not nuts. "Usually" is doing work in that sentence; ask every time.

Where shellfish hides

Shrimp is the visible shellfish and shrimp paste is the invisible one. Fermented shrimp paste goes into the broth of the central spicy beef noodle soup, into dipping sauces for fried tofu and boiled pork, into some stir-fried greens, and into a range of southern sauces. Fish sauce itself is made from fish, not shellfish, and is a separate allergen question; most shellfish allergies are to crustaceans, and fish sauce is anchovy.

Dried shrimp is sprinkled into salads, sticky rice and some soups the way peanuts are.

The crepe-like rice pancake is filled with shrimp; the fresh spring roll contains shrimp as standard; many "pork" dishes include shrimp as a second protein. The hiding places are the sauces and the broths, which are made in advance and cannot be altered at the table.

Cross-contamination

A street cart with one wok, one chopping board and one pair of tongs cannot keep shellfish away from your dish, and will not pretend to. A restaurant with a kitchen can, when told. For a severe allergy that is the dividing line: carts are for dishes that never contain the allergen and are cooked only in water, and restaurants are for everything else.

How to eat well anyway

The strategy that works is to settle on a short list of dishes you have confirmed safe and eat them in different places, rather than ordering new things in new places. Pho, grilled meats, rice plates and the bread sandwiches cover most of a trip for a peanut allergy.

For a shellfish allergy, lean north: northern cooking uses shrimp paste less than the centre and south, and the pho-and-grilled-pork repertoire there is largely shellfish-free, while Hue's cuisine is the hardest for a crustacean allergy in the country.

Hotel breakfasts, cooking classes and food tours are useful because you can brief one person in advance. Tell a food tour operator at booking; the good ones reroute the evening.

Vegetarian restaurants

Buddhist vegetarian restaurants, signed "chay", cook without fish, shellfish or shrimp paste by definition, and they exist in every town. For a shellfish allergy they are the easy option on a tired night. Peanuts still appear in them as a garnish, so the card still applies.

What to carry and where to go

Bring your own epinephrine auto-injectors for the whole trip, more than one, with the prescription and a doctor's letter for customs and airport security. Do not count on buying them in Vietnam. Keep antihistamines on you. In an emergency, call 113 for traffic police, 115 for an ambulance, or go straight to an international clinic.

In Hanoi, a government-published list names Family Medical Practice, International SOS and Raffles Medical as English-speaking clinics with emergency medicine, and the same groups operate in Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang; know the nearest one in each city before you need it.

Travel insurance covers an allergic reaction as a medical emergency; check that the policy does not exclude a pre-existing condition you did not declare, and declare it.

articles.title: Vietnam with Limited Mobility: Where It Works and Where It Does Not
articles.excerpt: Vietnam's pavements, boats and old towns are hard on anyone who walks with difficulty. The trip is still possible, and the way to make it work is to choose the places and the transport that fit.
articles.content:
Vietnam is a difficult country for a wheelchair user and a tiring one for anyone who walks with a stick, with a bad knee or with a parent in their eighties. The obstacles are specific: pavements used as motorbike parking, kerbs without ramps, bathroom doors narrower than a chair, and sights that involve stairs, boats and distance. None of that is a reason to stay home. It is a reason to plan the trip around what works, which is more than the pavements suggest.

The short version

Vietnam with limited mobility works when the trip is built on a car with a driver, hotels in the newer mid-range and upper brackets, and a shortlist of flat, compact places. It does not work as a backpacking trip, a motorbike trip or a trip built on the sights that need stairs and boats.

Da Nang, Hoi An's old town, Ho Chi Minh City's centre, Hue's citadel and the Mekong's bigger towns are the reliable core; Sapa, the Ha Giang loop and the cave trips are not.

What Vietnamese people will do

Help, unasked, and lift. A wheelchair at a step or a boat will attract hands before you have finished looking for them. It is generous and it is not a substitute for a ramp, and for anyone who does not want to be lifted it is worth saying so early.

The transport that works

A car with a driver is the piece of equipment that makes Vietnam accessible, and it is the standard way a visitor with limited mobility sees the country. A driver takes you door to door, waits, helps with the chair, and removes the pavement problem for every journey that is not on foot. Within cities, ride-hailing cars do the same job for short hops; the apps let you request a larger vehicle, and the driver meets you at the kerb.

Taxis from the major companies are fine; motorbike taxis are not.

Trains are the transport to avoid: carriages are reached by steep steps from low platforms, corridors are narrow and the toilets are not usable from a chair. Domestic flights are the long-distance answer, and the airlines provide wheelchair assistance when it is requested at booking, which is a thing to confirm by phone rather than assume. Long-distance coaches are workable for someone who can climb a few steps and not otherwise.

Airports

The international airports have lifts, assistance desks and accessible toilets. The bottleneck is between the terminal and the hotel, where the fixed-fare airport taxi or a pre-booked car with a driver beats anything that needs a kerb.

The places that work

Hoi An's old town is flat, closed to cars for much of the day, and compact enough to cover slowly; the paving is uneven in places and the crowds thick in the evening, but it is the most rewarding walkable town in the country for anyone who tires easily. Da Nang has wide new pavements, a long beachfront with ramps, and hotels built this decade.

Ho Chi Minh City's central district is flat, with the main museums and the cathedral square within a short drive of each other and lifts in the larger buildings. Hue's citadel is flat ground with raised thresholds at the gates, which a helper can manage with a chair.

In the Mekong Delta, Can Tho's riverfront is level and the floating market is seen from a boat, which raises the boarding question but not a walking one. Nha Trang and Phu Quoc's resorts are built for guests who do not want stairs, and a beach week there is the easiest part of any itinerary.

Hanoi

Hanoi is harder: the Old Quarter's pavements are the most obstructed in Vietnam, and the sights are spread out. It still works from a car, with the Temple of Literature, the Ho Chi Minh complex and the lake front each a short drive apart and mostly level once inside. Walking the Old Quarter is the thing to drop, not the city.

The places that do not

Sapa is a town of steep streets with treks around it, and the terraces are seen on foot or from a motorbike. Ha Long Bay's cruise boats are boarded by tender and have stairs between decks; some operators will manage a chair with notice, and the cheaper boats will not. Ninh Binh's rowboats are stepped into from a low jetty, which a steady person with a helper can do and a wheelchair user cannot. The Cu Chi tunnels are tunnels.

The Phong Nha show caves have long staircases. The Hang Mua viewpoint is a climb of several hundred steps.

Temples and pagodas across the country have thresholds to step over, which is deliberate, and often a flight of steps at the gate. Most are worth seeing from the courtyard, and the courtyard is usually reachable.

The halfway cases

Someone who walks slowly but can manage a few steps and a boat with help has a much longer list than a wheelchair user: Ha Long with the right operator, a Ninh Binh boat, the Imperial City, the Marble Mountains by lift to the main level. The question to ask any operator is not "is it accessible" but "how many steps, and is there a handrail".

Hotels and bathrooms

The newer mid-range and upper hotels have lifts and some have rooms with wider bathroom doors and walk-in showers; the older guesthouses and the budget hotels have neither, and bathroom doorways too narrow for a standard chair are the norm outside the top tier. Ask for the bathroom door width and whether the shower is step-free, in writing, before booking, and book hotels in Vietnam from the international chains or the newer resorts where that answer is reliable.

Toilets in town

Accessible public toilets are rare. Hotel lobbies, the larger shopping malls, and international-standard restaurants are the dependable options, and a day out should be planned around them.

Planning the trip

Build the itinerary as a loop of the places that work, joined by flights and a driver, and give each one more days than a fit traveller would, because the point is to be there rather than to cover it.

Da Nang and Hoi An, then Hue by car over the pass, then a flight south to the city and a driver into the delta, with a beach week at the end, is a two-week trip that asks for no stairs that cannot be avoided. Specialist agencies that arrange accessible travel in Vietnam exist and know which hotels and boats will actually manage a chair; using one is cheaper than finding out on arrival.
